text: is_incremental decides which rows get selected. incremental_strategy decides what dbt does with those rows once selected. Three strategies cover almost every case: merge, delete+insert, and append.

Merge is the default, and usually the right call. It compiles to a real MERGE statement — the same one you already know from T-SQL and Snowflake: match on unique_key, update if it exists, insert if it doesn't. Correct whenever individual rows can change after they first arrive.

Delete+insert deletes every row in the target whose key shows up in the new batch, then inserts the new batch wholesale, instead of matching field-by-field. Better when a whole batch naturally replaces a whole prior batch, or on warehouses where MERGE is slow or unsupported.

Append just inserts the new rows — no matching, no unique_key at all needed. Cheapest by far, and correct only for genuinely append-only data like immutable event logs. Use it on data that can be updated later and you get duplicate rows the moment a changed row looks new.
Rows updated after arrival: merge. A batch replacing a whole prior batch: delete+insert. Truly immutable event data: append. That's the entire decision.
